body.heading: No such thing as suck
paragraphs: Strictly speaking, a vacuum cleaner does not suck anything. Its motor spins a fan that constantly throws air out of the machine, keeping the pressure inside lower than the pressure of the room. Air abhors an imbalance, so outside air rushes in through the nozzle to equalise it.

That inrushing air is the working stream: it sweeps across the carpet, carrying dust, crumbs and hair with it. The push comes from the atmosphere itself, which presses on everything at sea level with a force of about ten tonnes per square metre.

body.heading: Catching the dirt, freeing the air
paragraphs: The dirty air passes through a bag or a filter — in bagless designs, a spinning cyclone flings the heavier dirt outward into a bin while the air spirals on. The cleaned air then flows over the motor, cooling it, and out of the exhaust.

Fine filters called HEPA filters trap particles a fraction of the width of a hair, including much pollen and dust-mite debris. As any filter clogs, the airflow weakens — the machine sounds willing but cleans less, which is why emptying and washing filters matters.

body.heading: Why the nozzle matters
paragraphs: Cleaning happens where the airstream is fastest and closest to the dirt, so nozzle design matters as much as motor power. A rotating brush bar beats carpet fibres to loosen embedded grit into the airstream, which is why vacuuming works better than the suction figure suggests.

Robot vacuums use the identical physics with a fraction of the power, compensating with patience — passing over the same floor many times. The principle has not changed in a century: make a pressure difference, and let the atmosphere do the pushing.

description: A vacuum cleaner doesn't suck: its fan lowers the pressure inside, and the air outside pushes itself — and dirt — in.
